passage:
"Someone must have called already," Pankaj said, looking at the scooter lying on its side near the crossing and the rider on the road. About thirty people stood in a ring. Some held up phones.
"Did you call?" asked Sarika.
"No. I thought..."
"Everyone thinks that." She pointed. "You, in the blue shirt, call 112 and tell them the crossing near the bakery. You, with the cap, stop the cars. Pankaj, stay by him and talk. Nobody move him."
Pankaj crouched. "Can you hear me? Help is coming." The man in the blue shirt was already speaking to the operator.

qa.q: Where was the scooter lying?
qa.a: The scooter was lying on its side near the crossing.

qa.q: What is Pankaj feeling when saying that someone must have called already?
qa.a: Pankaj is probably shocked and unsure, and hopes that someone else has taken charge, which lets Pankaj avoid acting.

qa.q: What broke the crowd's waiting, and why did it work?
qa.a: Sarika pointed at specific people and gave each a task, such as calling 112 and stopping cars, so nobody could assume someone else would.

qa.q: How might the rider feel hearing Pankaj say "Help is coming"?
qa.a: The rider might feel frightened but comforted that a person is nearby speaking calmly, instead of a ring of people only watching.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a crowd assuming someone else has called for help until one person names who should call.

passage: I was at the bus stop by the flyover when a man near the shelter dropped to the ground. A crowd formed. I stood at the back, holding my school bag, thinking someone had surely phoned. Phones were up, but I could not see anyone speaking into one. Then Minakshi, who sells tea at the stall, called across, "You with the bag. Call 112. Say the bus stop by the flyover." My hands shook, but I dialled. The operator asked simple questions and told me to stay on the line. Minakshi sat beside the man and kept talking to him. I kept thinking how long I would have stood there. Jagdish

qa.q: Who told the narrator to call 112?
qa.a: Minakshi, who sells tea at the stall, told Jagdish to call 112.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling while standing at the back holding the school bag?
qa.a: Jagdish was probably unsure and frozen, assuming that someone else had surely phoned.

qa.q: What made Jagdish finally act?
qa.a: Minakshi picked Jagdish out of the crowd and gave a clear instruction to call 112 and say the bus stop by the flyover.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have seen the crowd standing around?
qa.a: Minakshi could see that people had phones up but nobody speaking to an operator, so gave a direct order to one person.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a crowd assuming someone else has called until a person is named to call.

passage:
PE teacher's note, inter-school athletics meet, Saturday.
During the 800-metre race, a runner from another school collapsed near the stands. Within seconds, about thirty students crowded around. I saw Uday, one of our Class 10 boys, standing at the front with his phone in his hand, looking at the runner. Nobody was calling. Later he told me, "I thought someone must have already called." I pushed through, knelt by the runner and pointed at him: "Uday, you. Call 108 now. Tell them the school ground on Ring Road." He dialled at once. I asked Manjula ma'am to clear the crowd. The ambulance came in twelve minutes. On Monday I will talk to the class about why naming one person matters.

qa.q: How many students crowded around the runner?
qa.a: About thirty students crowded around.

qa.q: What was Uday thinking while he stood with his phone?
qa.a: He assumed someone must have already called, so he felt no push to act and stood frozen, unsure.

qa.q: Why did the teacher point at Uday by name?
qa.a: Naming one person broke the shared assumption that someone else would call, so Uday dialled at once.

qa.q: How might the collapsed runner have been affected if no one had been named?
qa.a: Help might have come much later, since everyone in the crowd assumed someone else had already called.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager in a crowd assuming someone else had called for help until he is named to call.

passage:
Dear Diary, Tuesday.
Something happened near the bus stop today that I keep thinking about. An old man on a scooter skidded and fell. People gathered, maybe twenty of us. Everyone was looking. I thought, someone has surely called the ambulance already. I didn't move.
Then Sharmila didi, who works at the pharmacy, came out and pointed straight at me. "You. Call 108. Tell them outside the Shiv Mandir bus stop." My hands shook but I did it. She sent two other boys to stop the traffic. The ambulance came.
Afterwards I realised: nobody had called. Everyone thought someone else had. That could have been Dadaji.
Omkar

qa.q: Where did the old man fall?
qa.a: Near the bus stop, outside the Shiv Mandir bus stop.

qa.q: What was Omkar thinking before Sharmila didi pointed?
qa.a: Omkar assumed someone had surely called the ambulance already, and felt unsure and hesitant, so did nothing.

qa.q: What broke the crowd's inaction?
qa.a: Sharmila didi pointing at one person to call 108 and sending others to stop the traffic.

qa.q: How might the old man have been affected if no one had been named?
qa.a: He might have lain there much longer, since everyone assumed someone else had called.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows a crowd at an accident where everyone assumes someone else called, until one person is named.

passage: At the Thursday market in a village outside Dharwad, a tractor trolley reversing too fast knocked over the potato stall, and its owner went down under the planks. In seconds twenty people stood in a ring. Sudha, sixteen, clutching her mother's shopping bag, stared at the man's leg twisted under the wood. Someone must have called by now, she thought. Everyone had phones out. Nobody was dialling; they were filming or muttering. Then Samir, the schoolteacher who ran the seed shop, pushed through and pointed straight at her. "You, green dupatta. Call 108. Say Thursday market, near the water tank." Sudha's fingers shook, but she dialled. Samir pointed at two men: "You two, lift only the planks, slowly. Nobody move him." The operator asked questions and Sudha answered each one, reading landmarks off the signboard. She stayed on the line until the siren came up the dusty road.

qa.q: How many people stood in a ring around the fallen stall?
qa.a: Twenty people.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling and assuming before Samir pointed at her?
qa.a: She was shocked and frozen, assuming someone must already have called because everyone had phones out.

qa.q: Why did Samir's pointing work when the crowd did nothing?
qa.a: Naming one person with one clear task made the responsibility hers, so it no longer felt shared by everyone and done by no one.

qa.q: What is it like for the stall owner while twenty people only film?
qa.a: He is hurt and trapped under the planks while people watch, so he is likely frightened and alone until someone finally calls and help comes.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a crowd at an accident assuming someone else has called, until being named as the one to call breaks the spell.
